meta.title: The potential adverse effects of hypodermic glucagon-like peptide -1 receptor agonist on patients with type 2 diabetes: A population-based study.
meta.abstract:
Background

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), a class of injectable antidiabetic drugs, have shown significant efficacies in improving glycemic and weight control in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, the long-term safety of GLP-1 RAs remains insufficiently studied. This study aimed to provide real-world evidence on potential adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use in T2D patients without major chronic diseases including impaired cardiac or renal function.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study involving 7746 T2D patients on GLP-1 RAs in Shenzhen, China. They were compared with 124 371 metformin-only users and 36 146 insulin-only users, forming two therapy control groups. GLP-1 RAs users were also further 1:2 paired with the control groups. Competing risk survival analyses were conducted to assess the incidence risks, presenting subdistributional hazard ratios (sHRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for various adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use.

Results

Compared with metformin-only users, GLP-1 RAs use was associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes (sHRs with 95% CIs), including pancreatitis (2.01, 1.24-3.24), acute nephritis (3.20, 2.17-4.70), kidney failure (3.73, 2.74-5.08), thyroid cancer (2.25, 1.23-4.10), and thyroid dysfunction (1.27, 1.00-1.63), respectively; Similar results were also found when compared with insulin-only users. Importantly, long-term (≥12 months) GLP-1 RAs use may further elevate the incidence risks of pancreatitis, acute nephritis, thyroid cancer, and thyroid dysfunction.

Conclusion

Compared with traditional T2D treatments, GLP-1 RAs use may be associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes in a Chinese population. Cautions were strongly warranted in the use of GLP-1 RAs. Further validation is crucial across diverse populations.

domains.name: Confounding
domains.direction_justification: GLP-1 RA users had substantially higher baseline obesity (BMI 30.0–39.9 kg/m²: 13.21% vs 3.04% in insulin and 4.87% in metformin; Table 3S) and higher socioeconomic/insurance coverage (citizen health insurance: 75.60% vs 54.96% in metformin; Table 3S). Critical clinical confounders were unadjusted or largely missing (HbA1c missing in 91.27%, FPG missing in 33.22%, and baseline eGFR/triglycerides unmeasured), and propensity score matching matched participants on an 'unspecified' missing category for ~33% of BMI and ~20% of age (Table 1), leaving severe unmeasured and residual confounding that artificially inflates risk estimates away from the null.

findings.title: Unmeasured and residual confounding by disease severity, baseline organ function, and metabolic parameters
findings.mechanism: Key risk factors for pancreatitis (e.g., hypertriglyceridemia, alcohol use), renal disease (baseline eGFR, proteinuria, ACEi/ARB use), and thyroid cancer (family history, prior neck radiation) were not measured or controlled. Furthermore, HbA1c had a 91.27% missing rate at baseline (Table 1, footnote a).
evidence: Missing rate for HbA1c was 91.27% and for Fasting Plasma Glucose was 33.22% (Table 1 footnote)
Baseline BMI 30.0-39.9 kg/m² was 13.21% in GLP-1 RAs vs 4.87% in metformin and 3.04% in insulin (Table 3S)

findings.title: Propensity score matching on missingness indicator categories
findings.mechanism: PSM included large proportions of 'unspecified' categories as matching levels (e.g., 33.81% vs 36.08% unspecified BMI, 20.53% vs 21.93% unspecified age; Table 1). Matching on missing categories fails to balance the actual underlying continuous covariates, resulting in pseudo-balance and residual confounding.

Education Unspecified: 33.62% in GLP-1 RA vs 35.89% in Insulin paired cohort (Table 1)

domains.direction_justification: Exclusion of 362,035 out of 985,278 patients due to missing prescription data and restriction to patients maintaining monotherapy throughout follow-up selects for distinct clinical trajectories and creates immortal time / selection bias that exaggerates rate differences away from the null.

domains.name: Post-exposure interventions
domains.direction_justification: Differential switches or discontinuation following minor adverse events were treated as competing risk events rather than standard time-varying confounding.

findings.title: Definition of mild acute side effects as competing risks
findings.mechanism: Defining mild symptoms (dizziness, diarrhea, acne) as competing risks in a Fine-Gray model rather than censoring or handling via time-varying survival methods can distort subdistribution hazard ratios.
evidence: Competing events systematically defined as a binomial variable activated by any incidence of specific acute symptoms including diarrhea/emesis, acne, dizziness, arrhythmia (Methods 2.3)

domains.name: Missing data
domains.direction_justification: Over 90% of glycemic control data (HbA1c: 91.27% missing) and ~33% of baseline anthropometrics/demographics were missing and maintained as distinct categories, preventing true confounding control and biasing risk estimates away from the null.

findings.title: Extensive missingness in key laboratory and clinical variables
findings.mechanism: Complete case analysis or categorical missing indicators were used for missing covariates with extreme missingness, leading to substantial bias.
evidence: HbA1c missing rate: 90.52% in GLP-1 RAs, 91.79% in insulin, 90.45% in metformin (Table 3S note)
Fasting plasma glucose missing rate: 32.95% in GLP-1 RAs, 32.66% in insulin, 24.13% in metformin (Table 3S note)

domains.name: Measurement of the outcome
domains.direction_justification: GLP-1 RA users had higher citizen insurance coverage (75.60% vs 54.96% in metformin; Table 3S) and higher education levels (26.07% vs 11.94% undergraduate; Table 3S), leading to greater diagnostic scrutiny (detection bias) for subclinical conditions (e.g., thyroid nodules/cancer, asymptomatic nephritis/renal failure, sHR: 2.25 and 3.73), pushing estimates away from the null.

findings.title: Surveillance and diagnostic workup bias
findings.mechanism: Patients initiating expensive injectable therapies (GLP-1 RAs) undergo more frequent outpatient biochemical monitoring, ultrasound surveillance (thyroid, abdomen), and clinical workup than patients maintained on oral metformin, increasing the incidental detection rate of thyroid cancer, thyroid dysfunction, and renal abnormalities.
evidence: Outcomes identified via regular expression match on unstructured text and ICD-10 diagnostic codes across outpatient and inpatient records (Table 2S)
Citizen health insurance: 75.60% in GLP-1 RAs vs 54.96% in metformin (Table 3S)
Undergraduate education: 26.07% in GLP-1 RAs vs 11.94% in metformin (Table 3S)

domains.name: Selection of the reported result
domains.direction_justification: Multiple outcomes and post-hoc duration cutoffs (e.g., <12 vs ≥12 months) were evaluated without a published prospective protocol, elevating the probability of selectively highlighting extreme effect estimates (e.g., leukemia sHR 15.09; Figure 3).

findings.title: Multiple outcome testing without pre-registered statistical analysis plan
findings.mechanism: Evaluation of dozens of discrete ICD-10 categories and exploratory subgroup cutoffs without multiplicity correction increases false positive findings.
evidence: More than 18 distinct disease outcomes tested across 4 individual drug sub-cohorts and 2 duration stratifications without multi-testing adjustment (Methods 2.2, Figures 2-3, Figures 1S-10S)

overall.summary: The study is at very high risk of bias under the ROBINS-E framework. The observed associations between GLP-1 RA use and elevated risks of adverse outcomes (including pancreatitis, acute nephritis, renal failure, thyroid cancer, and leukemia) are heavily confounded and distorted by selection and surveillance mechanisms. Major limitations include conditioning exposure definitions on long-term monotherapy across follow-up (immortal time/selection bias), massive missingness in essential clinical confounders (HbA1c missing in >90% of subjects; baseline eGFR/triglycerides unmeasured), matching propensity scores across large 'unspecified' missing categories, and profound surveillance/detection bias driven by higher socioeconomic status, insurance coverage, and diagnostic workups among GLP-1 RA recipients.

unresolvable_without_more_data: Raw event counts for each adverse outcome per treatment arm (the manuscript only reports sample sizes and sHRs with 95% CIs, omitting 2x2 contingency tables).
Baseline kidney function (eGFR/creatinine) and lipid profile (triglycerides) to evaluate baseline pancreatitis and nephropathy confounding.
Proportion of thyroid cancer and renal failure cases detected via routine/incidental screening vs symptomatic clinical presentation.

baseline_comparability.summary: At baseline, GLP-1 RA users were substantially younger and higher-educated but carried a higher prevalence of obesity and healthcare insurance coverage compared to insulin and metformin comparators. Because key clinical confounders (diabetes duration and baseline HbA1c, which was >90% missing) were not controlled, baseline surveillance differences and residual confounding push effect estimates for rare adverse outcomes away from the null.

time_related_biases.summary: The study defines exposure retrospectively across the entire follow-up rather than using an incident new-user design at treatment initiation. The lack of a latency lag period in a cohort with only 23.7 months mean follow-up creates strong reverse causation and detection bias for slow-onset outcomes like thyroid cancer and leukemia.
